wine.name: Felton Road Block 5 Pinot Noir
wine.grapes: Pinot Noir alone, from one block of The Elms Vineyard.
wine.sites: Block 5 of The Elms Vineyard at Bannockburn, planted in 1993 on a north facing slope whose soils run from heavy loess and silt to clay and angular schist gravel, with old lake bed sediments reaching into its centre.
wine.making: Destemmed by gravity into the fermenters, with about a fifth kept as whole bunches in a vintage such as 2017, the fruit soaks for more than a week before a wild fermentation with indigenous yeasts, some three weeks on skins in all. It then spends sixteen to seventeen months in French oak barrels, a quarter to about a third of them new, and goes to bottle unfined and unfiltered.
wine.glass: Dark cherry, raspberry and crushed berries over rose petal, rhubarb, black tea and white pepper; darker and spicier than the house's other Pinot Noirs, with a stony edge, muscular yet fine tannin and a long finish.
wine.ageing: Tight and muscular when young, it needs four or five years to open and then drinks well for a decade or more.
wine.serve: 15 to 17 degrees Celsius; decant a young bottle for an hour or so; a wide Burgundy glass.

label.means: One block of The Elms Vineyard, planted in 1993 and bottled on its own.
The sub-region of The Elms, on old gold sluicings above the Kawarau arm of Lake Dunstan.
The registered Geographical Indication of the inland south of New Zealand's South Island.

records.table: Felton Road Block 5 is Bannockburn Pinot Noir from one north facing block of The Elms Vineyard, planted in 1993 and farmed biodynamically. Darker and spicier than the house's other Pinots, it is tight when young, so give it four or five years and decant it.
records.story: In 1990, by New Zealand Winegrowers' account, Felton Road's founder enrolled in the viticulture course at Lincoln University, and in 1991, the year the house dates its beginning to, he chose and laid out a vineyard on a north facing slope just off Felton Road at Bannockburn, a district of old gold sluicings above the Kawarau. The first vines went in in 1992, and Block 5 followed in 1993 in what became The Elms Vineyard. In 1997 a young winemaker who had been the founder's laboratory partner at Lincoln made the first official Felton Road Pinot Noir, and in 2000 the founder sold the estate to a British wine lover. The house came to bottle the blocks of The Elms apart, Block 3 and Block 5 above all, and to farm its vineyards biodynamically, certified by Demeter and by BioGro, wild yeasts in the cellar and no fining or filtering at the end. Block 5's soils run from loess and silt to clay and schist gravel, with old lake bed sediments at its heart, and its wine is the darker and spicier of the two. For a sommelier the pair is a lesson in how far soil alone can move Pinot Noir within one vineyard.

report: Founded 1991 agrees with the library; the house's own sheets date site selection and vineyard design to 1991, Block 2 to 1992 and Block 5 to 1993, and New Zealand Winegrowers has the founder enrol at Lincoln in 1990, plant The Elms and see the first official Pinot Noir made in 1997, which the library's region record also gives.

Living people kept out: the founder (spelled Stewart and Stuart in the sources, not yet in people.json), the winemaker of 1997 and the buyer of 2000 (both already in people.json); the sale of 2000 rests on New Zealand Winegrowers and the Otago Daily Times, the buyer called British by the newspaper.

The making gathers the house's sheets by vintage: about a fifth whole bunch, a pre-fermentation soak of eight to ten days and twenty one to twenty three days on skins in 2017, sixteen months with thirty per cent new oak in 2017 and twenty five per cent in 2021, sixteen to seventeen months by the Block 3 and Block 5 sheet; hand picking was not confirmed and is not said.

The glass and ageing draw on the house's own notes (darker fruited and spicier than its other Pinots, a mineral note) and the critics its product pages quote (raspberry, rhubarb, rose petal, dark cherry; crushed berry, tea, white pepper; muscular tannin; four or five years to open, windows of about five to fifteen years from the vintage).
One merchant listing dates Block 5's first release to the 1999 vintage; with no second source the record gives no first year for the block's own bottling.

The library's region line and record call Felton Road the region's benchmark and its reference producer; the record does not, since the tab refuses a judgement, and the library's semi-continental in the traps sits beside the region record's continental, a small tension left for the integrator.
No swap proposed: the pick is right for the region.

records.place: Roy's Bay, Lake Wanaka, Central Otago

wine.name: Rippon Mature Vine Pinot Noir
wine.grapes: Pinot Noir alone, from every fully grown Pinot Noir vine on the estate.
wine.sites: The north facing escarpment above Roy's Bay on the western shore of Lake Wanaka, where terminal moraines and coarse gravels, all of schist, meet; by the house's account its blocks include some of the oldest commercial vines in Central Otago.
wine.making: Fermented with a share of whole bunches that the house sets by each vintage's fruit, the wine spends two winters in barrel, about eighteen months, and then two more years in bottle before it is released. It goes to bottle without fining or filtering.
wine.glass: Wild strawberry, dark cherry and plum over blueberry, mountain herbs and a note of mushroomy undergrowth, with crushed rock beneath; juicy and elegant rather than heavy, with fine, chalky tannin and a long, perfumed finish.
wine.ageing: Released with years in bottle already, it is open and perfumed on release, and in a strong vintage it keeps and deepens for a decade and more.
wine.serve: 15 to 17 degrees Celsius; no need to decant, though a young bottle opens in a carafe; a wide Burgundy glass.

label.means: Drawn from all the estate's fully grown Pinot Noir vines, the younger ones left out.
The northernmost sub-region of Central Otago, moderated by the lake, and the estate's address.
The registered Geographical Indication that covers every sub-region of the inland south.

records.table: Rippon Mature Vine Pinot Noir comes from every fully grown vine on a schist and glacial gravel slope above Lake Wanaka, where the family planted trial vines in 1975. Fine and perfumed, it spends two winters in barrel and two years in bottle before release.
records.story: The Mills family has farmed the land at Roy's Bay on Lake Wanaka since 1912, by its own account. The founder had thought of growing grapes there since coming home from the Second World War, in which he served as a submarine lieutenant, and in 1973 he and his wife moved back to the family farm. In 1975 he planted a trial of some thirty grape varieties beside the lake, among the first vines of modern Central Otago, and in 1982, against the doubts of research bodies and local experts, he planted the first commercial block, the year from which the house dates its winegrowing. He became the first president of the Central Otago Grape Growers Association, the forerunner of the region's winegrowers' association. After his death his widow carried on the business they had founded, and their son went on to lead the vineyard and the cellar. The estate is farmed biodynamically, and Mature Vine gathers all of its fully grown Pinot Noir, while two single blocks, Tinker's Field and Emma's Block, are bottled apart. For a sommelier, Rippon carries the modern region's story back to its trials of the 1970s: Pinot Noir from a lakeside farm where the vines began as an experiment.

Rippon's trial vines of 1975 came before the region's first commercial vintage of 1987, but its first commercial block was planted only in 1982.
Lake Wanaka is Central Otago's northernmost sub-region, moderated by the lake, and no part of Gibbston or the Cromwell Basin.

report: The house is not in the library: founded is 1982, the first commercial block, the year the house dates its winegrowing from and New Zealand Winegrowers gives for commercial planting; the trial of 1975 is in both, and the region line's trials of the 1970s and commercial vineyard of the 1980s agree.

The founder is described, not named: his death in 2000 is in several pages read through one search summary, but no source gave his birth year, so he cannot be named with his dates; his widow and their son, who leads the estate, are living and kept out, neither yet in people.json.

The release regime rests on two secondary sources: the World of Fine Wine's vertical (eighteen months in barrel, two years in bottle) and the Wine Advocate's note quoted by Flatiron Wines (two winters in barrel, two in bottle); the house's pages read here gave no making.

Left out for want of a second source: hand picking into small cases, fifteen to twenty per cent new oak in the first winter, whole bunches of twenty five to forty per cent, and own rooted blocks of the 1980s and 1990s, each in one listing only; unfined and unfiltered is in two merchant notes (Vino Fino of 2022 and a critic's note of 2023).

The glass draws on Wine Enthusiast's review of the 2019 (currant, blueberry, florals, undergrowth, dried herbs), the Halliday Wine Companion's note of the 2023 (plum, wild strawberry, dark cherry, crushed rock, mountain herbs) and the Wine Advocate's chalky tannin; the ageing on windows of about a decade and more in those reviews.
A young vine Pinot Noir of the house was not confirmed in any source read, so others lists only the single blocks and the Riesling, and no second wine is named.

The association's later name is said as the region's winegrowers' association, since the summary gave it as the Central Otago Wine Association and the body styles itself the Central Otago Winegrowers Association.
No swap proposed.

wine.name: Gibbston Valley Reserve Pinot Noir
wine.grapes: Pinot Noir alone, from the house's own vineyards.
wine.sites: A few low yielding rows chosen in a strong vintage from the house's vineyards: the Home Block at Gibbston in the Kawarau Gorge, planted in 1983, and its sites at Bendigo, among them the higher China Terrace and School House.
wine.making: As the house tells it, a Reserve takes only a few rows of fruit in a great vintage and is made in small quantities, apart from its other Pinot Noirs. The house publishes no fixed recipe for it; its barrels of Pinot Noir and Chardonnay rest in the cave blasted into the schist behind the winery in 1995.
wine.glass: Black cherry and wild strawberry over pomegranate and cranberry, with violets and roses, a creamy cola note and clove, nutmeg and cinnamon from the barrel; more textured and lush than the house's other Pinot Noirs.
wine.ageing: Generous enough to drink on release, it gains depth over several years in bottle in a strong vintage.
wine.serve: 15 to 17 degrees Celsius; decant a young bottle for an hour if you wish; a wide Burgundy glass.

label.means: The house's selection of a few rows of fruit in a strong vintage, made in small quantities.
The house's name, from Gibbston, the highest and coolest sub-region of Central Otago, in the Kawarau Gorge.
The registered Geographical Indication of the region, whose first commercial vintage came from this house in 1987.

records.table: Gibbston Valley released Central Otago's first commercial vintage in 1987, and its Reserve Pinot Noir is the house's pick of a few rows in a strong year. Its 2000 vintage took the Pinot Noir trophy at the International Wine Challenge in London.
records.story: Gibbston lies in the Kawarau Gorge between Queenstown and Cromwell, the highest and coolest corner of Central Otago. The house's founder planted his first vines there in the early 1980s, and in 1983, by the house's account, he planted its first commercial vineyard, the Home Block. In 1987 Gibbston Valley released the region's first commercial vintage, a date New Zealand Winegrowers gives for Gibbston's first commercial bottling. In 1990 the founder established Gibbston Valley Wines as a boutique winery with a tasting room and a restaurant, and by 1995 the barrels had outgrown their store; rather than build another, he had a cave blasted into the schist hill behind the winery, New Zealand's largest wine cave by the house's own account. The house came to grow at Bendigo too, on the warmer terraces by Lake Dunstan, where China Terrace and School House give its single vineyard wines. The Reserve is its selection of a few rows in a strong year, and the Reserve Pinot Noir of 2000 won the Pinot Noir trophy at the International Wine Challenge in London. For a sommelier the Reserve carries the region's early history: the first commercial vintage, the cave and a London trophy.

report: Founded is empty: the house's pages give 1983 for its first commercial vineyard and its establishment, and 1990 for the founding of Gibbston Valley Wines as a boutique winery; the story tells both.

The library says 1981: the region producers line (planted in 1981), the region record's milestone card (1981 Gibbston Valley and Black Ridge planted) and js/data-field-atlas.js's Gibbston lesson note; the house's history and two secondary pages (High Garden Vineyard and another) give 1983 for the Home Block, so the record says the early 1980s for the first vines and 1983 for the first commercial vineyard.
The founder is living and described, never named, and not yet in people.json; his Irish birth is in one secondary page only and is left out.

The 2000 Reserve's trophy at the London International Wine Challenge rests on the house's history page, Olivers Wines and an Altitude Tours page (which dates it 2001 and calls it a first outside Burgundy, a claim with no second source, left out).

The making is thin: no source read gave the Reserve's fermentation, oak or months in barrel; the house's newsletter figure of ten months in French oak, fifteen per cent new, names no wine and is not used. The refuter may wish to find a technical sheet or weigh a swap to School House Pinot Noir, whose sheets are published.

The glass draws on tasting notes of the 2014 Reserve on Delectable (cola, black cherry, strawberry, pomegranate, cranberry, roses and violets; more textured and lush, clove, nutmeg and cinnamon), one site only; the ageing is the author's judgement and says little.
The cave's date, its barrels and its size rest on the house's pages; Broadsheet and New Zealand Winegrowers' winery page also call it the country's largest wine cave.

wine.name: Mt Difficulty Bannockburn Pinot Noir
wine.grapes: Pinot Noir alone, a blend of clones, chiefly 5, 6 and 10/5.
wine.sites: Estate vineyards and vineyards the winery manages on the south side of the Kawarau at Bannockburn, the earlier plantings above all, on soils that run from open gravels to heavier clays.
wine.making: Lots of different clones are fermented together where the house can, and the wine then rests about twelve months in barrel on its full lees, going through its malolactic fermentation in the spring before it is racked out of barrel in late autumn. It is filtered but not fined.
wine.glass: Red and black cherry, raspberry and blood plum over blueberry and orange peel; fuller and darker than the cooler sub-regions give, with a silky texture, firm, fine grained tannin and bold acidity.
wine.ageing: Approachable on release, it keeps and deepens for some seven years and more in a strong vintage.
wine.serve: 15 to 17 degrees Celsius; decant a young bottle for an hour; a wide Burgundy glass.

label.means: The sub-region of all its vineyards, a registered Geographical Indication of its own since 2022.
The region's registered Geographical Indication, inside which Bannockburn lies.

records.table: Mt Difficulty Bannockburn Pinot Noir blends the house's vineyards on gravel and clay south of the Kawarau, where a group of growers began making wine under one label in 1998. Cherry and blood plum with silky, firm tannin, it is Bannockburn's warmth in a glass.
records.story: Bannockburn's terraces on the south side of the Kawarau were worked for gold in the nineteenth century, and its vineyards lie on the old sluicings. Vines came in the 1990s, when the owners of a handful of newly planted vineyards there, who called themselves the Gang of Four, chose to make wine together under one label rather than each alone. Mt Difficulty's first vintage was 1998. The growers' handshake held until 2004, when the company Mt Difficulty Wines was formed and the founding vineyards came into it. The house went on to bottle some of its vineyards apart: Pipeclay Terrace, from vines planted in 1996 on one of the four original vineyards along Felton Road, is released only in strong vintages, and Mansons Farm is made in small quantities. A second label, Roaring Meg, came to stand beside the first. In 2022 Bannockburn became a registered Geographical Indication of its own, the first sub-region of Central Otago to do so. For a sommelier, the Bannockburn Pinot Noir is the house's map of the sub-region in one bottle: fruit from many vineyards on gravel and clay, blended to show the place rather than one site.

report: The house is not in the library: founded is 1998, the first vintage, in the Otago Daily Times and a Glengarry Wines newsletter (WL114); the growers' handshake became the company Mt Difficulty Wines in 2004 by Supermarket News and a second Otago Daily Times piece.

Living people kept out, none yet in people.json: the founding grower and his wife, who planted several of Bannockburn's first vineyards, their son the long serving winemaker and the winemaker of Gibbston Valley who made the first vintages; pages with their names in the address (The Central App, Rural News) were read but not cited.

The making, sites and clones rest on the house's own fact sheets of 2016, 2018 and 2021 (co-fermented clonal lots in 2021); no sheet read gave the oak's origin or its share of new barrels, so the record says barrel alone.

The glass draws on the house's note of the 2024 and 2022 quoted by Vino Fino (red and black cherry, blueberry, blackberry, satsuma plum, silky fine tannin), Decanter's review of the 2017 (ripe plummy fruit) and New Zealand Winegrowers' line that Bannockburn gives fuller, more tannic Pinot Noir; the ageing on a critic's window of 2030 and more for the 2023.

Roaring Meg as the second label is in Supermarket News and a Woolworths listing; that it is named for the stream of the Kawarau Gorge is one page's account and Wikipedia's page on the gorge confirms the stream, so the note says named for, a tie the refuter should test.

Left out for want of a second source: a gold medal for the 1998 Pinot Noir at the Air New Zealand Wine Awards of 1999, the winery of 2001, the cellar door of 2003, the barrel hall of 2012, the growers' earlier sales of grapes to Gibbston Valley and Chard Farm, and a sale of the company in 2018 to an American buyer.

New Zealand Winegrowers' winery page says the winery was designed for low energy use with its barrel hall sunk below ground; left out of the story, since the five sources the cap allows went to the dates and the making.
No swap proposed: the Bannockburn Pinot Noir is the house's main Pinot Noir; its single vineyard wines come only in some vintages.

wine.name: Quartz Reef Bendigo Estate Pinot Noir
wine.grapes: Pinot Noir alone, grown on the house's own estate at Bendigo.
wine.sites: The Bendigo Estate vineyard, first planted in 1998 on a north facing slope above the east bank of Lake Dunstan, on arid clay, fine gravel and quartz over the reef that names the house; certified biodynamic by Demeter since 2011.
wine.making: Picked by hand and cold soaked, the fruit is fermented with indigenous yeasts and a small share of whole bunches, some twenty four days on skins in a vintage such as 2014. It then spends about fourteen months in French oak barriques, a quarter to a half of them new by vintage, and the 2017 went to bottle unfined and unfiltered.
wine.glass: Black cherry and ripe plum over violet and a hint of cedar, deep in colour and very savoury; weighty and dense, as the warm Bendigo slope makes it, with fine tannin and a long finish.
wine.ageing: Firm and youthful at first, it opens a few years after the vintage and keeps for a decade in a strong year.
wine.serve: 15 to 17 degrees Celsius; decant a young bottle for an hour; a wide Burgundy glass.

label.means: The house's own vineyard at Bendigo Station, first planted in 1998.
The sub-region on the east bank of Lake Dunstan, under the Dunstan Mountains, with the warmest terraces of Central Otago.
The registered Geographical Indication of the inland south, at about 45 degrees south.

records.table: Quartz Reef Bendigo Estate Pinot Noir grows over a quartz reef on a warm, north facing slope at Bendigo, first planted in 1998 and farmed biodynamically. Black cherry, plum and violet, dense yet savoury, it comes from a house known as well for its sparkling wine.
records.story: In 1996, by the house's account, an Austrian born winemaker founded Quartz Reef with two partners, a Cromwell businessman and the farmer of Bendigo Station, who had marked out the slopes of Bendigo, on the east bank of Lake Dunstan, as new ground for Central Otago. The house took its name from the quartz reef that runs beneath the vineyard, by its own account the largest quartz deposit in New Zealand. The first vines went into Bendigo Station in 1998, and the first harvest came in 2001. Beside its Pinot Noir the house made sparkling wine by the traditional method, with a second fermentation in bottle, and became known for both. In 2007 it began to convert the vineyard to biodynamic farming, and in 2011 it gained Demeter certification, with its winery certified organic by BioGro. The estate bottles single blocks of the vineyard apart, as its Single Ferment Pinot Noirs, while the Bendigo Estate Pinot Noir gathers the slope. For a sommelier it is the warm end of Central Otago in a glass: dark, dense Pinot Noir from a slope that faces the sun.

others.name: Quartz Reef Méthode Traditionnelle
others.note: The house's sparkling wine, made by a second fermentation in bottle, as Champagne is.

others.name: Quartz Reef Bendigo Estate Single Ferment Pinot Noir

traps: Quartz Reef is at Bendigo in Central Otago, New Zealand, not in the gold town of Bendigo in Victoria, Australia.
The Single Ferment Pinot Noirs are single blocks of the Bendigo estate, fermented apart; they are not the Bendigo Estate Pinot Noir itself.
Quartz Reef's sparkling wine is made by the traditional method, a second fermentation in bottle, not in tank.

questions.q: Which soils does Quartz Reef name for the north facing slope of its Bendigo Estate vineyard?
opts: Arid clay, fine gravel and quartz
Deep loess over lake bed silt
Glacial moraine and coarse schist gravel
Volcanic ash over limestone
questions.exp: The house describes its Bendigo slope as arid clay, fine gravel and quartz; moraine and coarse schist gravel describe Rippon's slope above Lake Wanaka instead.

questions.q: Quartz Reef was founded in 1996. In which year did the first vines go into Bendigo Station?
questions.exp: The first vines went in in 1998 and gave a first harvest in 2001; 1996 is the founding and 2007 the start of the biodynamic conversion.

report: The house is not in the library: founded is 1996, as the house's story page and the secondary pages read (Glengarry Wines, Vind, Fine Wine Delivery) give it and as the region line has it; the house's home page says 1998, the year of planting, and the house's timeline puts the start of the biodynamic conversion in 2001 where its other pages and the secondaries say 2007.

Living people kept out, none yet in people.json: the Austrian born founding winemaker and his two partners, a Cromwell businessman and the farmer of Bendigo Station; the critic whose review the house reprints is not named, and New Zealand Winegrowers' page on the founder is not cited because its address names him.

The making gathers the house's own pages by vintage: hand picked, a cold soak, indigenous yeasts with a small share of whole bunches, twenty four days on skins and fourteen months with twenty four per cent new barriques in 2014, half new and unfined and unfiltered in 2017; the 2004 was fined with egg white, so no habit of never fining is claimed.

The glass draws on the reviews the house reprints of the 2017 (deep, fragrant, weighty, very savoury, ripe cherry and plum) and the 2018 (black cherry, dark berry, violet, fine tannin), and on the library's dense Bendigo Pinot Noir; the ageing on Decanter's windows of about three to ten years from the vintage.
One secondary page calls the reef gold bearing; with no second source the record does not say so.

Left out for want of a second source: that sparkling wine was the founder's fallback while Pinot Noir was unproven, and that it makes up about three quarters of what the house bottles; the library's region line calls the house's sparkling the region's leading, a judgement this record does not repeat.

The plan's wine name is kept, though the house labels its Pinot Noirs variously as Bendigo Estate, Bendigo Estate Single Vineyard and Bendigo; the refuter may confirm the label of the vintage in question.
No swap proposed.
